title: Factoring Quadratic-Type Polynomials
short: Treat x⁴ − 5x² + 4 as a quadratic in x².

blocks.html: Some polynomials of degree 4 or 6 are really quadratics in disguise. It is the chunk idea again, combined with the trinomial factoring you learned in Factoring Completely.

If the powers are $x^{2n}$, $x^n$ and a constant (like $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$), let $u = x^n$. Factor the quadratic in $u$, put $x^n$ back, then check each factor again: differences of squares and cubes may split further.

$x^4$ is $(x^2)^2$, so $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ is exactly $u^2 - 5u + 4$ with $u = x^2$. Any factoring of the quadratic in $u$ is a true identity for every value of $u$, including $u = x^2$. The substitution only changes how it looks.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $y = x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ $= (x - 1)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 2)$ has four zeros, one for each linear factor.

blocks.title: A factor that stops
blocks.q: Factor $x^4 + x^2 - 12$ completely over the integers.
steps: $x^2 + 4$ is a sum of squares and $3$ is not a perfect square, so neither factor splits over the integers.

blocks.title: Cubes inside
steps: Each is a difference of cubes: $x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1)$ and $x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)$.

blocks.html: Stopping after the $u$ step. $(x^2 - 1)(x^2 - 4)$ is equal to the original, but it is not factored completely. After putting $x^n$ back, look at every factor again.
